questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the MODERN PERIODIC TABLE. 1. Moseley corrected Mendeleev by ordering elements by atomic NUMBER rather than atomic mass. 2. The table has 7 periods and 18 groups. 3. Lanthanides and actinides are placed together as f-block elements below the main table. 4. Noble gases have zero electron affinity because they have a complete octet. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: All four are correct. Moseley (1913) reordered by atomic number, fixing anomalies like Ar-K and Co-Ni. Table has 7 periods, 18 groups. f-block (La-Lu, Ac-Lr) is split out below for space. Noble gases have effectively zero electron affinity — they don't want to gain electrons (stable octet).

questions.stem: Arrange the following in order of INCREASING first ionization energy: Na, Mg, Al, Si.
questions.explanation: Trend across period 3: Na (495 kJ/mol) < Mg (737) > Al (577) < Si (786). Mg > Al is the ANOMALY — Mg has filled 3s², while Al's lone 3p¹ is easier to remove. Hence Na < Al < Mg < Si.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched with its periodic-trend description?

options.option_text: Atomic radius — decreases across a period left to right
Metallic character — increases across a period left to right
Ionization energy — generally increases across a period

questions.explanation: Metallic character DECREASES across a period (metals on the left, non-metals on the right) and INCREASES down a group. The other three trends are correctly described. Negative-stem distractor.

questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): Fluorine has a higher electronegativity than chlorine. REASON (R): Fluorine's smaller atomic size means the bonding electrons are held more tightly to its nucleus.

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.explanation: Fluorine (Pauling EN 3.98) vs Chlorine (3.16) — F is the most electronegative element. The physical reason is exactly its small atomic size — the bonding pair sits very close to the nuclear charge. Correct A + R with R being the right explanation.

questions.stem: An element X has atomic number 17. Which of the following is TRUE about X?

options.option_text: X is a halogen and exists as a diatomic molecule X₂.
X is a noble gas with completely filled valence shell.

questions.explanation: Z = 17 → Chlorine. Configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ (option D shows 3p⁴ which is wrong — that would be sulphur Z=16). Chlorine is group 17 halogen, exists as Cl₂. Yellow-green pungent gas. Used for water disinfection.

questions.stem: Match the element with its special property. A. Element with the HIGHEST electronegativity. B. Only metal LIQUID at room temperature. C. Lightest metal. D. Most ABUNDANT element in Earth's crust. List-II: 1. Oxygen. 2. Lithium. 3. Mercury. 4. Fluorine.
questions.explanation: F is the most electronegative. Hg is the only metal liquid at room temperature. Li is the lightest metal (density 0.534 g/cm³). Oxygen is 46 % of Earth's crust by mass (most abundant element in crust). Four classic 'superlative' facts students must keep straight.

questions.stem: Consider the following group-16 (chalcogens) statements. 1. Oxygen is gaseous; sulfur, selenium and tellurium are solids at room temperature. 2. Oxygen exhibits a maximum oxidation state of +2 in compounds. 3. Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) is a stronger acid than water. 4. Ozone (O₃) is an allotrope of oxygen. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 2 is WRONG — oxygen generally exhibits a −2 oxidation state; its positive states are very rare (with fluorine only, e.g. OF₂ where O is +2). The broader descriptor 'maximum +2' is misleading. Statements 1, 3, 4 are correct. (H₂S pKa ≈ 7 vs water pKa ≈ 15.7 — H₂S is a stronger acid; ozone is a well-known allotrope of oxygen.)

questions.stem: A student claims: 'All elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell.' This statement is:

options.option_text: True for main-group (s- and p-block) elements, but NOT strictly for transition and inner-transition metals

questions.explanation: For s/p-block (groups 1, 2, 13-18) the claim holds cleanly. For d-block (transition metals) the differentiating electron enters a d-sub-shell of (n−1) — so outermost-shell count is less predictive, and oxidation behaviour varies within a group. For f-block it's yet more complex. This nuance is a common exam trap.
